P2-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors

Sinuo Wang Affiliation: Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China    Jiacheng Lu Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China    Zeyu Zhang Affiliation: Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia    Maojia Song Affiliation: Singapore University of Technology and Design, Singapore    Rui Sun Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China    Beidi Luan Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China    Yutong Xie Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates    Jing Li Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China    Daxin Jiang Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China    Qi Wu Affiliation: Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia Correspondence to: qi.wu01@adelaide.edu.au    Zuo Bai Affiliation: StepFun, Shanghai, China Correspondence to: baizuo@stepfun.com
Abstract

Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P2-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P2-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P2-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD. Code is available at https://github.com/SinuoWang/P2-MOPD.

Keywords: 
On-Policy Distillation, Model Merging, Task Arithmetic, Large Language Models
††affiliationnotice: †Co-corresponding authors. ‡Project lead.

1 Introduction

Frontier large language models are increasingly built by training separate domain experts, often with domain-specific reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026), and then consolidating them into a single generalist. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) (Ma et al., 2026a), in which each teacher supervises the student’s own responses in its domain, has become a standard recipe for this step (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026b; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026a; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; NVIDIA, 2026; Kimi Team, 2026). Ideally, the consolidated model retains the capability of every expert, rather than trading one domain for another. Because MOPD benefits from supervising the student’s own behavior, its pipeline is heavy. Every step samples rollouts from the student and runs each teacher over them with teacher forcing to obtain token-level labels, and the student must approach each teacher’s performance through many such steps. Prior work has also found that MOPD does not recover all domains evenly (Kim et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). Even when it starts from a merge of the experts, it can leave one domain far behind, and continued distillation can erode a capability that the merge already had. The other common way to consolidate experts is model merging. Task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023) adds a weighted sum of the experts’ task vectors to the base model without any training. Because the behavior of the merged model is never supervised, its quality is not guaranteed. In our experiments, for instance, a uniform merge recovers less than half of the gap between the base model and the teachers (Table 1).

Task arithmetic falls short on its own, but its partial success is informative. If a training-free linear combination of the experts already recovers part of their capabilities, their parameters encode a useful prior for the consolidated model. We take this observation one step further. A linear combination of the base student and the frozen experts is itself a single model, differentiable in both its mixing coefficients and the student’s weights, and can therefore be trained end to end under the MOPD objective. Viewed this way, the experts no longer serve only as an initialization or a one-off merge but act as parameter priors throughout training, so the student need not climb the whole way to each teacher on its own. Based on this view, we propose P2-MOPD (Parameter-Prior MOPD; Figure 2). It keeps the MOPD loss and its supervision on the student’s own trajectories, but parameterizes the student as a linear combination of its own trainable weights and the frozen expert parameters (Equation 4). The student thus receives two kinds of guidance from the experts under a single loss: their logits supervise its outputs, as in MOPD, and their parameters enter its weights through the mixing coefficients, which the on-policy loss updates together with the student weights. Unlike task arithmetic, P2-MOPD keeps the base student’s weights fully trainable, so the consolidated model is not confined to the span of the student and expert parameters. Such confinement would be restrictive, since task vectors of separately trained experts interfere with each other (Yadav et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024), and with only KK directions per module the merged model can trade one domain against another but cannot make adjustments that none of the experts contains. In P2-MOPD, the mixing coefficients move the model along expert-derived directions and the weights adapt it beyond them. The closest prior work, IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026), also reuses the expert parameters but merges task vectors into the student at fixed points according to an external validation rule, whereas P2-MOPD learns the combination continuously from the distillation gradient.

To understand why learning the combination helps, we project each model’s change onto the task vectors (Section 4.3). MOPD from the merged start moves the student along most task vectors but hardly along that of the expert whose domain it leaves behind. P2-MOPD moves an order of magnitude farther along this direction, and across methods the recovery of that domain tracks the movement. The learnable coefficients thus make reachable a teacher-aligned direction that student weight-only updates do not take, while the weights adapt the student outside the span of the task vectors, so the two channels divide the work.

Across four domains (medicine, law, finance and instruction following) at two scales, P2-MOPD is both faster and more balanced than MOPD from the same merged start (Section 4.2). After half the training steps, it already exceeds the final average recovery of MOPD at lower wall-clock cost (Figure 1), and at the end of training it raises worst-domain recovery from below half to nearly 90%90\%. Learning the mixing coefficients alone, inside the span, falls far short, so both the expert prior and the freedom to leave its span are needed (Section 5). Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose P2-MOPD, which treats a linear combination of the student and frozen experts as a single model and trains its weights and mixing coefficients jointly under the MOPD objective (Section 3).

  • •

    Student weight-only MOPD updates barely move along the direction of the lagging expert; the learnable coefficients make this direction reachable, while the weights adapt the student beyond the task-vector span (Section 4.3).

  • •

    At two scales, P2-MOPD surpasses the final average recovery of MOPD in half the training steps and raises worst-domain recovery from below 50%50\% to nearly 90%90\% (Sections 4.2 and 5).

2 Related Work

Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation.

On-policy distillation (OPD) (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026) supervises the student with teacher feedback on its own trajectories and has become a dense-reward alternative to reinforcement learning in LLM post-training. MOPD (Ma et al., 2026a) extends OPD to consolidating several RL-trained domain experts by routing each prompt to the teacher of its domain, and is used in recent frontier technical reports to consolidate domain experts into one model (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026b; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026a; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; NVIDIA, 2026; Kimi Team, 2026). Follow-up work refines which teacher supervises which token and how strongly, through budget balancing across domains (Gao et al., 2026), label-free token routing (Xu et al., 2026), or soft-prompt teachers (Ma et al., 2026b). These methods improve the supervision but treat the student as a plain set of weights. Closest to ours, IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026) shows that the expert parameters themselves also help: it initializes the student by task arithmetic and periodically merges task vectors of under-recovered domains back into it. However, these merges are rule-based and rely on an extra validation signal rather than the distillation gradient. P2-MOPD instead treats the linear combination of trainable student parameters and frozen expert parameters as a single differentiable model, jointly optimizing the student weights and expert mixing coefficients throughout training under the same on-policy objective.

Model Merging.

Model merging combines experts in weight space without training, for example by task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023) and its interference-reducing variants (Yadav et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024). Because good fixed coefficients are hard to choose, another line learns them: AdaMerging (Yang et al., 2024) fits task- or layer-wise coefficients by entropy minimization on unlabeled test data, and subsequent methods learn them from task data, expert logits or expert activations (Zhang et al., 2024; Gauthier-Caron et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). Other work interleaves merging with training as a discrete step between phases (Choshen et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025). Together, these works show that trained expert parameters can be combined into a reasonable model even without training. They still treat merging as an operation that outputs a model, either offline or between training phases. Our view is different: since task arithmetic is a linear and fully differentiable function of its coefficients, the combination of student and expert parameters can be treated as one model. P2-MOPD trains this model inside MOPD, so the expert parameters serve as a prior and the on-policy objective updates both the mixing coefficients and the student weights, without confining the student to the span of the task vectors.

3 Method

P2-MOPD rests on a simple view. A linear combination of model parameters is itself a single model, whose forward pass uses only the composed weights, and the composition is differentiable in its mixing coefficients. P2-MOPD therefore reparameterizes the MOPD student as trainable student weights plus a learnable combination of frozen expert weights, and jointly optimizes the student weights and the mixing coefficients under the on-policy distillation objective (Figure 2). The experts thus guide the student in two ways: their logits supervise its behavior, and their weights serve as parameter priors. Section 3.1 defines the notation and objective, Section 3.2 introduces the parameterization, and Section 3.3 presents the update rule and its geometric interpretation.

3.1 Problem Formulation and Preliminaries

Experts and task arithmetic.

Let θ0\theta_{0} be a shared base model and θ1,…,θK\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{K} be KK domain experts obtained from θ0\theta_{0} by domain-specific post-training. The task vector of expert kk is τk=θk−θ0\tau_{k}=\theta_{k}-\theta_{0} (Ilharco et al., 2023), and a task-arithmetic (TA) merge is

θTA​(λ)=θ0+∑k=1Kλk​τk,\theta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\lambda)=\theta_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\,\tau_{k}, (1)

with coefficients λ∈ℝK\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{K} (uniform, λk=1/K\lambda_{k}=1/K, throughout this paper). TA is training-free, but the merge is confined to the KK-dimensional affine span of the task vectors.

Multi-teacher on-policy distillation.

MOPD trains one student πθ\pi_{\theta} on prompts xx with known domain labels d⁡(x)∈{1,…,K}d(x)\in\{1,\dots,K\}. At step tt the current student πθt\pi_{\theta_{t}} samples a response yy for each prompt, and the expert of the prompt’s domain, πθd⁡(x)\pi_{\theta_{d(x)}}, scores it. Let p⁡(v)p(v) and q⁡(v)q(v) denote the student’s and the routed teacher’s next-token distributions at position ii. Following the top-kk form of MOPD (Ma et al., 2026a) as implemented in Open-MOPD (Gao et al., 2026), each candidate vv in a student-defined support 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} (top-SS student tokens with a nucleus cut; Appendix A) receives the reward

ri​(v)=−wi​(v)​[log⁡p⁡(v)−log⁡q⁡(v)],v∈𝒱i,r_{i}(v)=-\,w_{i}(v)\,\big[\log p(v)-\log q(v)\big],\qquad v\in\mathcal{V}_{i}, (2)

with wi​(v)=p⁡(v)/∑u∈𝒱ip⁡(u)w_{i}(v)=p(v)/\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}p(u), a support-restricted reverse-KL signal (Appendix A). The rewards are treated as constants (sg\operatorname{sg}), and the student is updated with a clipped policy-gradient surrogate. Since every rollout batch is used for one optimizer update, the update direction is the gradient of

ℒt​(θ)=−1Nt∑(x,y)∈ℬt∑i∈y∑v∈𝒱isg⁡[ri​(v)]​log​πθ​(v∣x,y<i)\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{N_{t}}&\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}\ \sum_{i\in y}\ \sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}\\ &\operatorname{sg}\!\big[r_{i}(v)\big]\,\log\pi_{\theta}(v\mid x,y_{<i})\end{split} (3)

at θ=θt\theta=\theta_{t}, where ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} is the rollout batch and NtN_{t} its number of unmasked response tokens. Standard MOPD applies this gradient to all parameters of a student initialized at θ0\theta_{0}, at an SFT warm-up, or at the TA merge θTA​(λ)\theta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\lambda), which we denote MOPD, MOPD (SFT warm-up) and MOPD (TA init) (Ma et al., 2026a; Kim et al., 2026); in MOPD (TA init) the task vectors enter only through the initial point.

3.2 Expert Parameters as Differentiable Priors

Parameterization.

P2-MOPD is applied module-wise. A module m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} is one linear projection of a decoder layer (query, key, value and output in attention; gate, up and down in the MLP). The remaining tensors ϕ\phi (token embeddings, normalization weights and the output head, including a tied embedding) are trained as in MOPD. For a module m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} let Wm(k)W^{(k)}_{m} be the corresponding tensor of expert kk, with task vector τk,m=Wm(k)−Wm(0)\tau_{k,m}=W^{(k)}_{m}-W^{(0)}_{m}. P2-MOPD parameterizes the student’s module weights as

Wm​(B,α)=Bm+∑k=1Kαk,m​τk,m,m∈ℳ,W_{m}(B,\alpha)=B_{m}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{k,m}\,\tau_{k,m},\qquad m\in\mathcal{M}, (4)

where the full tensors B={Bm}m∈ℳB=\{B_{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}} and the scalar mixing coefficients α∈ℝK×|ℳ|\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times|\mathcal{M}|} are both trainable and the task vectors are frozen (left block of Figure 2). No gradient is back-propagated into any teacher network: the teachers enter the loss only through the constant rewards, and the task vectors enter the parameterization only as fixed directions. Since BB is unconstrained, Equation 4 represents exactly the same models as a plain student. What it changes is how the student moves: a single scalar step on αk,m\alpha_{k,m} moves the whole module along a task vector. In this sense the frozen experts act as parameter priors, a bias on the optimization path rather than on the model class (Section 3.3).

Coefficient granularity.

Equation 4 gives every module its own KK coefficients (module granularity, K​|ℳ|K|\mathcal{M}| scalars). The coefficients can also be tied across modules: at layer granularity all projections of one decoder layer share KK coefficients, and at model granularity there is one coefficient per expert (KK scalars), the learnable analogue of Equation 1. Tying only constrains α\alpha; every module keeps its own task vectors and weights. It is implemented by writing the full table as α=α~​T⊤\alpha=\tilde{\alpha}\,T^{\top} for a fixed binary assignment matrix TT and optimizing the free parameters α~\tilde{\alpha}, so the gradient of a tied coefficient is the sum of the gradients of the modules it covers. Our main experiments use module granularity; the method does not depend on it, and finer tying is not necessarily better (Sections 5 and 6).

Initialization.

P2-MOPD starts from the TA merge θTA​(λ)\theta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\lambda), in which every tensor (modules and ϕ\phi alike) is merged with the TA coefficients λ\lambda. It sets Bm=Wm(0)B_{m}=W^{(0)}_{m} and αk,m=λk\alpha_{k,m}=\lambda_{k}, so that Wm​(B,α)W_{m}(B,\alpha) reproduces the merged module weights exactly, and takes ϕ\phi from the merge. Equivalently, at initialization Wm=(1−∑kαk,m)​Wm(0)+∑kαk,m​Wm(k)W_{m}=(1-\sum_{k}\alpha_{k,m})\,W^{(0)}_{m}+\sum_{k}\alpha_{k,m}\,W^{(k)}_{m}: a linear combination of the base and expert weights whose coefficients remain learnable for the entire run.

Gradients.

Let Gm=∂ℒt/∂WmG_{m}=\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}/\partial W_{m} be the ordinary gradient of the distillation loss with respect to the composed weight, evaluated at the current weights. By the chain rule through Equation 4,

∂ℒt∂Bm=Gm,∂ℒt∂αk,m=⟨Gm,τk,m⟩.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial B_{m}}=G_{m},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\partial\alpha_{k,m}}=\big\langle G_{m},\,\tau_{k,m}\big\rangle. (5)

The coefficient gradient is the directional derivative of the loss along the frozen task vector: a negative value means that, to first order, increasing module mm’s contribution from expert kk decreases the current batch loss. Because the batch contains prompts of all domains, every coefficient receives a sum of contributions from all domains, ⟨Gm,τk,m⟩=∑d⟨Gm(d),τk,m⟩\langle G_{m},\tau_{k,m}\rangle=\sum_{d}\langle G^{(d)}_{m},\tau_{k,m}\rangle, not only from the domain of expert kk.

3.3 Joint Optimization and Its Interpretation

Update rule.

Equation 4 is the conceptual model: it defines α\alpha and gives the coefficient gradient through the chain rule. The optimizer, however, does not maintain BB. It maintains the materialized weights WW in full precision and advances them with a two-channel step (Algorithm 1; the two backward paths of Figure 2):

Wt+1=AdamWηW⁡(Wt,clipcW​(Gt))+∑k(αt+1−αt)kτk,\begin{split}W_{t+1}={}&\operatorname{AdamW}_{\eta_{W}}\!\big(W_{t},\,\mathrm{clip}_{c_{W}}(G_{t})\big)\\ &+\sum_{k}\big(\alpha_{t+1}-\alpha_{t}\big)_{k}\,\tau_{k},\end{split} (6)

where αt+1=Adamηα⁡(αt,clipcα​(D⊤​Gt))\alpha_{t+1}=\operatorname{Adam}_{\eta_{\alpha}}\big(\alpha_{t},\mathrm{clip}_{c_{\alpha}}(D^{\top}G_{t})\big) and D⊤​GtD^{\top}G_{t} collects the inner products of Equation 5. Three details of Equation 6 matter. (i) Both channels consume the same pre-update gradient GtG_{t}, computed once at θt\theta_{t}; there is no second backward pass. (ii) The coefficient gradient is taken from GtG_{t} before the weight gradient is clipped, and the two channels are clipped separately, so neither channel’s clipping budget is consumed by the other. (iii) The student weight channel uses no weight decay, so running AdamW on the materialized WW and adding the coefficient increment is identical to running the same optimizer on BB and recomposing W=B+∑kαk​τkW=B+\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}\tau_{k}, because GtG_{t} is the same for WW and BB by Equation 5 (Appendix B). The non-ℳ\mathcal{M} parameters ϕ\phi follow the AdamW channel alone. The per-step displacement of a module is therefore

Δ​Wm=ΔmAdamW⏟student weight channel+∑kΔ​αk,m​τk,m⏟∈span⁡{τ1,m,…,τK,m}.\Delta W_{m}=\underbrace{\Delta^{\operatorname{AdamW}}_{m}}_{\text{student weight channel}}+\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{k}\Delta\alpha_{k,m}\,\tau_{k,m}}_{\in\,\mathrm{span}\{\tau_{1,m},\dots,\tau_{K,m}\}}. (7)

At module granularity the second term lies, for each module, in a subspace of dimension at most KK; over the whole network the coefficient channel moves within a structured subspace of dimension at most K​|ℳ|K|\mathcal{M}|, while the first term is unrestricted and moves both inside and outside that subspace. Coarser tying (layer, model) replaces the per-module span by the smaller span of stacked task vectors, dimension at most K​LKL or KK.

Parameter priors as preconditioning.

Like reparameterizations that leave the model class unchanged but alter the optimization geometry (Salimans & Kingma, 2016; Arora et al., 2018), the two channels can be read as one preconditioned step (Amari, 1998). Fix one module, write w=b+D​αw=b+D\alpha with D=[vec​τ1,…,vec​τK]D=[\mathrm{vec}\,\tau_{1},\dots,\mathrm{vec}\,\tau_{K}], and let g=∇wℒtg=\nabla_{w}\mathcal{L}_{t} for a fixed batch. If both channels used plain SGD, with no momentum, no clipping and no decay, then Δ​b=−ηW​g\Delta b=-\eta_{W}g and Δ​α=−ηα​D⊤​g\Delta\alpha=-\eta_{\alpha}D^{\top}g, hence

w+=w−(ηW​I+ηα​D​D⊤)​g.w^{+}=w-\big(\eta_{W}I+\eta_{\alpha}DD^{\top}\big)\,g. (8)

The parameter prior thus acts as a preconditioner: a positive semidefinite term of rank at most KK amplifies the gradient component along the task vectors, with strength set by ηα\eta_{\alpha} relative to ηW\eta_{W} (under layer or model tying, DD is replaced by the stacked task vectors of the tied group). Adam and clipping act on each channel separately, so Equation 8 describes the direction of the change, not its size; Section 4 measures its effect.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models and data.

We follow the protocol of IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026) at two scales, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-1.7B. The base θ0\theta_{0} is the general SFT reference model of that work, and at each scale four domain teachers (medical, law, finance, instruction following) are fine-tuned from the same θ0\theta_{0}, so the task vectors τk=θk−θ0\tau_{k}=\theta_{k}-\theta_{0} are well defined. The domains are evaluated on MedQA, CaseHOLD, FinQA and IFBench. We omit the fifth domain, τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al., 2025), because its user simulator requires a paid commercial LLM API. Every training batch contains 128 prompts, 32 from each domain, and each prompt is distilled from the teacher of its domain. Teacher provenance, prompt pools and test splits are given in Appendix C.

Methods.

MOPD (TA init) is the primary control: MOPD from the uniform TA merge (λk=0.25\lambda_{k}=0.25), that is, P2-MOPD with the mixing coefficients α\alpha frozen at λ\lambda (the ηα=0\eta_{\alpha}=0 corner of Algorithm 1). MOPD starts from θ0\theta_{0} and MOPD (SFT warm-up) from an SFT warm-up on teacher samples. Open-MOPD (Gao et al., 2026) adds per-domain budget balancing, and IM-MOPD (Kim et al., 2026) periodically merges the task vectors of under-recovered domains into the student; both start from the same merge. P2-MOPD uses module-wise granularity unless stated otherwise.

Training and evaluation.

All experiments run on eight GPUs (Appendix F). Every run trains for 100 steps of one rollout batch each, the training budget of IM-MOPD; we call the checkpoint at step 100 the final checkpoint. Checkpoints at steps 25, 50, 75 and 100 are scored with the official IM-MOPD evaluation harness, which samples three responses per test item with evaluation seeds 42, 43 and 44 and averages their scores (avg@3; Appendix G). Per-domain recovery is (s−sbase)/(steacher−sbase)(s-s_{\mathrm{base}})/(s_{\mathrm{teacher}}-s_{\mathrm{base}}); the headline metric is the average recovery over the four domains, and the worst-domain recovery measures balance. Because the base-to-teacher spans differ by up to a factor of three across domains, we report raw scores alongside. P2-MOPD, MOPD (TA init) and IM-MOPD are also trained with three training seeds at both scales; we report their means and standard deviations over the three training runs and compare P2-MOPD and MOPD (TA init) in pairs of runs with the same training seed.

4.2 Main Results

Faster recovery.

Figure 1 compares P2-MOPD with MOPD (TA init), which differs from it only in freezing the mixing coefficients α\alpha at their TA values. P2-MOPD is ahead from the first checkpoint, by +6.2+6.2 (4B) and +21.5+21.5 (1.7B) average-recovery points at step 25, and stays ahead in all 24 seed-paired comparisons (two scales, three seeds, four checkpoints; Appendix G). After half the training steps it reaches 92.392.3 (4B) and 90.590.5 (1.7B), already above the final average recovery of MOPD (TA init) (83.183.1 and 80.980.9) in every seed pair, and the advantage carries over to wall-clock time (Section 4.4). The two scales differ in how the gap evolves. At 4B it widens at every checkpoint, to +11.7+11.7 at the end of training. At 1.7B it emerges at the first checkpoint, and P2-MOPD continues to recover gradually.

Final performance.

At the end of training P2-MOPD leads at both scales in average recovery (Table 1) and in mean raw score, by +2.66+2.66 (4B) and +2.17+2.17 (1.7B) points (paired, three seeds); the raw gain is positive in every seed. P2-MOPD also ends well above MOPD and MOPD (SFT warm-up), and above IM-MOPD at both scales, with non-overlapping seed ranges (93.593.5–97.297.2 versus 86.686.6–89.289.2 at 4B, 94.294.2–95.895.8 versus 59.059.0–77.477.4 at 1.7B). At 1.7B, IM-MOPD’s end point depends on which domains its validation-gated rule happens to merge, and its average recovery varies by 1818 points across seeds.

Balanced recovery.

The clearest effect is on the worst-recovered domain (Figure 3). For MOPD (TA init) this is almost always MedQA, while the other three domains are recovered about as fast as by P2-MOPD (Figure 3b, c). At 1.7B, MOPD (TA init) even ends below the MedQA recovery of the TA start (44%44\%) in all three seeds: continued distillation erodes a capability the merge already had. P2-MOPD closes this gap from the first checkpoint and ends with a worst-domain recovery of 89.489.4 (4B) and 88.088.0 (1.7B), against 47.247.2 and 32.032.0 for MOPD (TA init), while the across-domain std of recovery falls from 21.821.8 to 4.64.6 (4B) and from 28.428.4 to 4.84.8 (1.7B). IM-MOPD is also balanced at 4B (worst domain 84.184.1), where every seed merges the medical teacher at step 25, but it first exceeds 80%80\% average recovery only at step 50 or 75, against step 25 for P2-MOPD; at 1.7B its worst domain is 48.748.7.

Where the gain comes from.

Table 2 breaks the average-recovery difference down by domain. The gain is concentrated where MOPD (TA init) falls short: MedQA is higher in every seed-paired comparison at both scales, by +29.0+29.0 (4B) and +48.2+48.2 (1.7B) recovery points on average, several times the difference in any other domain. CaseHOLD is mostly higher by small margins. On FinQA, which MOPD (TA init) already recovers almost fully, P2-MOPD is slightly lower in most pairs, and IFBench differs in both directions with a large spread across pairs. These differences lie around a high level: at the end of training P2-MOPD recovers on average at least 88%88\% of the teacher gap in every domain, including 98%98\% (4B) and 94%94\% (1.7B) on FinQA (Table 1), and the small FinQA deficit reflects the competition for αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} analysed in Section 4.3. P2-MOPD thus lifts the domain that MOPD leaves behind while keeping every other domain close to its teacher.

4.3 Why Learnable Coefficients Help

Task-vector projection.

To see where each method moves the student, we project the displacement of every module from the TA start onto the span of its four task vectors, in units of α\alpha (Appendix C). MOPD (TA init) does use the task vectors, but unevenly: it moves +0.09+0.09 to +0.13+0.13 along τlaw\tau_{\mathrm{law}}, τfin\tau_{\mathrm{fin}} and τif\tau_{\mathrm{if}}, and only +0.03+0.03 along τmed\tau_{\mathrm{med}}, the direction of the domain it fails to recover, at both scales and in every seed (Figure 4). P2-MOPD moves farthest along exactly this direction, by +0.40+0.40 (4B) and +0.42+0.42 (1.7B), 13–15 times as far. Within P2-MOPD, the two channels divide the work: the coefficient channel accounts for 81%81\% (4B) and 84%84\% (1.7B) of the displacement energy, whereas the student weight channel moves almost entirely outside the span (only 1.7%1.7\% and 4.0%4.0\% of its displacement lies inside). The same projection also accounts for MedQA across methods. Among the final checkpoints of P2-MOPD, MOPD (TA init) and IM-MOPD at both scales, the three that recover MedQA above 84%84\% all moved at least 0.300.30 along τmed\tau_{\mathrm{med}}: P2-MOPD at both scales through its coefficients, and 4B IM-MOPD through merging the medical teacher at step 25. The other three moved at most 0.030.03: MOPD (TA init) at both scales, and 1.7B IM-MOPD, which did not merge the medical teacher. Recovering the lagging domain thus coincides with a large step along its task vector, a step that student weight-only updates do not take and that P2-MOPD takes through one coefficient per module.

Conflict resolution in coefficient space.

P2-MOPD turns cross-domain interference into a contest over a few interpretable scalars, settled continuously by the gradient in favour of the lagging domain. The per-domain coefficient gradients show where the conflict lives: the medical gradient lies 98% on αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} and has cosine −0.78-0.78 / −0.63-0.63 with the finance / IF gradients at 4B (−0.85-0.85 / −0.81-0.81 at 1.7B), so the domains disagree mainly about one scalar per module. They also show how it is settled: at every step the medical gradient pushes αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} up while the finance and IF gradients push it down, their sum follows the medical gradient, and αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} rises from 0.250.25 to 0.630.63 (4B) and 0.650.65 (1.7B). The price is paid by the domains that lose this contest, and it is small: a slight FinQA deficit and mixed IFBench differences (Table 2), against a far more balanced recovery overall (Figure 3). The student weight channel is what makes this resolution possible. With the weights frozen, the coefficients alone must serve all four domains and do not favour αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} (its lead over the mean of the other three is +0.06+0.06 / −0.07-0.07, against +0.20+0.20 / +0.22+0.22 in P2-MOPD); with the weights free to adapt the other domains, the coefficients can specialize on τmed\tau_{\mathrm{med}}. The conflict is real but does not explain the gap of MOPD (TA init), which we test by training on medical prompts alone (Table 3, 1.7B). Without the other domains, MOPD (TA init) still barely moves along τmed\tau_{\mathrm{med}} (+0.048+0.048, against +0.028+0.028 with four domains), its medical KL stays more than seven times that of P2-MOPD under the same change, and its MedQA recovery falls to −6.9-6.9. Inside P2-MOPD, removing the other domains adds only 3–9 points of MedQA recovery from step 50 on, small against the gap of 65 points to MOPD (TA init).

Isolating the medical direction.

The remaining explanation is reachability: MOPD (TA init) falls short on MedQA because student weight-only updates do not move along τmed\tau_{\mathrm{med}}. The other interventions in Table 3 separate this direction from the extra capacity that the coefficients add. If the gain came from extra trainable directions, any KK directions per module would serve; random directions in place of the task vectors do not beat MOPD (TA init) at any checkpoint. Learning only the αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} row, one scalar per module, recovers nearly all of the gain (95.095.0 versus 95.895.8 average recovery), and freezing αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} returns MedQA to the level of MOPD (TA init) (24.224.2 versus 22.122.1), so the gain follows the medical coefficient in both directions. Learning only αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} requires knowing in advance which domain lags; P2-MOPD learns all coefficients and finds this direction on its own. The learnable coefficients thus make reachable a teacher-aligned direction that student weight-only updates do not take, while the student weight channel adapts the other domains.

4.4 Training Cost

P2-MOPD adds only the coefficient table and its optimizer state (at most on the order of 10310^{3} scalars), and its output is a standard checkpoint with α\alpha folded into the weights, so inference is unchanged. Training makes each step more expensive but needs far fewer steps. The extra time comes from streaming the task vectors to compute the coefficient gradients and the composed update (Appendix B). This lengthens the actor update from 14.714.7 to 73.873.8 s at 4B and from 11.111.1 to 37.137.1 s at 1.7B. However, it is rollout generation, not the actor update, that dominates each step, so 100 steps of P2-MOPD take only 1.24×1.24\times (4B) and 1.09×1.09\times (1.7B) the wall-clock of MOPD (TA init). Table 4 converts this into the time needed to reach a fixed quality. MOPD (TA init) reaches its final average recovery (83.183.1 / 80.980.9) only at the end of its 100 steps. P2-MOPD already exceeds it at step 25 at 4B (85.485.4, 0.31×0.31\times the wall-clock) and at step 50 at 1.7B (90.590.5, 0.55×0.55\times); since checkpoints are 25 steps apart, these are upper bounds. Within the wall-clock of 100 steps of MOPD (TA init), P2-MOPD completes about 80 (4B) and 92 (1.7B) steps, and its step-75 checkpoint, which fits in this budget at both scales, reaches 95.795.7 / 89.389.3. From step 50 on, it also exceeds the best checkpoint of MOPD (TA init) at any step (85.885.8 / 80.980.9).

5 Ablation Studies

Inside versus beyond the task-vector span.

With the weights frozen, every module stays at Wm(0)+∑k(αk,m−αk,m(0))​τk,mW^{(0)}_{m}+\sum_{k}(\alpha_{k,m}-\alpha^{(0)}_{k,m})\tau_{k,m}: the student can only move within the span of the task vectors, and P2-MOPD reduces to learning the task-arithmetic coefficients by on-policy distillation. Training the weights as well lets the student leave the span. Table 5 and Figure 5 compare the two, together with the untrained TA start and MOPD (TA init), which trains the student weights with the mixing coefficients frozen. Learning the mixing coefficients inside the span improves on the TA start by +10.0+10.0 and +16.9+16.9 average-recovery points (4B / 1.7B), but stays far below P2-MOPD (+51.9+51.9 and +62.3+62.3), which also has the best worst-domain recovery at both scales. The step beyond the span is small but decisive: it carries only 14.6%14.6\% / 10.0%10.0\% of the displacement energy of P2-MOPD (Figure 4), yet allowing it is what separates P2-MOPD from the coefficients-only variant. Conversely, the student weight channel without learnable coefficients, MOPD (TA init), gains +40.2+40.2 and +48.5+48.5 points but leaves MedQA behind (Section 4.3). The coefficients thus move the student along teacher-aligned directions, the weights adapt it beyond their span, and only the combination gives the best average and worst-domain recovery. P2-MOPD is therefore more than a learned merge: the experts supply the directions, and the distilled model is free to leave the space that any merge of them can reach. The sensitivity to the coefficient learning rate is reported in Appendix D.

Coefficient granularity.

Table 6 compares module, layer and model granularity at the end of training. At 1.7B all three end between 9494 and 97%97\% average recovery, and layer tying ends with the lowest across-domain std (1.51.5). At 4B, model tying (96.596.5) falls within the seed range of module granularity (93.593.5–97.297.2), so the two cannot be separated, whereas layer tying ends at 73.473.4, about 2020 points below both. The 1.7B layer run does not show this drop. Model tying has the highest mean at both scales, but its across-domain std depends on the scale (3.63.6 at 4B, 9.39.3 at 1.7B). Module-wise granularity is the setting that combines high average recovery with a low across-domain std at both scales (average recovery 94.994.9 / 94.794.7, std 4.64.6 / 4.84.8). We therefore use it as the main setting.

Initialization.

The advantage of P2-MOPD over MOPD does not come from the TA start. At 1.7B we also start both methods from the base model (α0=0\alpha_{0}=0, so that ηα=0\eta_{\alpha}=0 is MOPD), with otherwise identical settings. P2-MOPD leads MOPD at every checkpoint and at both coefficient learning rates we tried (10−210^{-2} and 3×10−23\times 10^{-2}), ending at 61.261.2 and 66.266.2 average recovery against −15.7-15.7 (Appendix D). As from the TA start, most of the gain comes from MedQA. The expert priors therefore help even when the student does not start at the merge: P2-MOPD does not depend on a merged initialization to improve on MOPD, and it learns from the base student itself how much of each expert to draw on.

Learned coefficients.

The learned mixture is stable: after training, the mean coefficient of each teacher agrees across the three seeds to within 0.010.01, so the mixture is a structured outcome learned from the experts and the student. It also moves away from the uniform 0.250.25 in a consistent direction. The medical coefficient rises the most (to 0.630.63 at 4B and 0.650.65 at 1.7B, against 0.330.33–0.460.46 for the other three teachers; Table 9), toward the domain that MOPD (TA init) fails to recover (Section 4.3). When the weights are frozen, the coefficients have to absorb the whole update: they move much further (std over all module coefficients 0.380.38–0.400.40 versus 0.120.12–0.140.14), and some module coefficients become negative. Learned jointly with the weights, they stay a moderate mixture of the experts, because the student weight channel adapts what the task-vector span cannot express. The learned coefficients are thus a reproducible and interpretable by-product of training: without any validation data, they identify the teacher that the student most needs.

6 Conclusion

We proposed P2-MOPD, which treats a linear combination of the student and frozen experts as a single model and trains its weights and mixing coefficients jointly under the MOPD objective. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B, it surpasses the final average recovery of MOPD in half the training steps and raises worst-domain recovery from below half to nearly 90%90\%. The gain comes from reachability. Student weight-only updates barely move along the task vector of the lagging domain, whereas one learnable coefficient per module makes this direction reachable, and the student weight channel adapts the model beyond the task-vector span. The advantage persists without a merged initialization, and the learned coefficients consistently identify the teacher that the student most needs. More broadly, expert parameters need not be consumed once, as an initialization or a merge. Kept as learnable priors throughout distillation, they guide where the student moves, which makes expert weights, and not only expert predictions, a source of supervision for multi-teacher consolidation.

Appendix A The Distillation Objective as Implemented

This appendix states the exact objective behind Equations 2 and 3, as used in all reported runs.

Rollouts and log-probabilities.

At step tt the rollout engine holds the weights θt\theta_{t} synchronized after step t−1t-1. It samples one response per prompt at temperature 1.01.0 with top-p=1.0p=1.0 and no top-kk. After generation, the student log-probabilities used in the reward and in the importance ratio are recomputed by the learner with the same weights θt\theta_{t} (not read from the rollout engine), and the teacher log-probabilities are computed by the routed teacher πθd⁡(x)\pi_{\theta_{d(x)}} on the same prefixes at temperature 1.01.0.

Support.

At every response position ii, the support 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} is formed from the student distribution only (“student top-kk” strategy): the S=16S=16 most probable student tokens are selected; their probabilities are renormalized among themselves; and, in descending order, a token is retained while the cumulative renormalized mass preceding it is below 0.990.99 (so the token that crosses the threshold is kept and the most probable token is always kept). The teacher distribution is evaluated on the same support; tokens outside 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} contribute nothing. The support is rebuilt from the recomputed student log-probabilities at learner time.

Reward.

With wi​(v)=p⁡(v)/∑u∈𝒱ip⁡(u)w_{i}(v)=p(v)/\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}p(u) the per-candidate reward is ri​(v)=−wi​(v)​[log⁡p⁡(v)−log⁡q⁡(v)]r_{i}(v)=-w_{i}(v)[\log p(v)-\log q(v)] as in Equation 2, with raw (not renormalized) log-probabilities inside the bracket. Writing Zp=∑u∈𝒱ip⁡(u)Z_{p}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}p(u) and Zq=∑u∈𝒱iq⁡(u)Z_{q}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}q(u) for the support masses and p~,q~\tilde{p},\tilde{q} for the two distributions renormalized on 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i}, the summed reward is

∑v∈𝒱iri(v)=−[KL(p~∥q~)+logZpZq],\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}r_{i}(v)=-\Big[\mathrm{KL}\big(\tilde{p}\,\|\,\tilde{q}\big)+\log\tfrac{Z_{p}}{Z_{q}}\Big], (9)

i.e. a support-restricted reverse KL plus a term that penalizes the student for placing more mass on its own top candidates than the teacher does. Responses that hit the generation length cap are masked out. No reward-scale normalization and no target-share or budget correction is applied in the reported runs, except for the budget balancing of Open-MOPD. The reward is used directly as the per-candidate advantage (Ai​(v)=ri​(v)A_{i}(v)=r_{i}(v), no baseline, no group normalization), and it is recomputed at learner time from the recomputed student log-probabilities.

Surrogate.

Let ρi​(v)=πθ​(v∣x,y<i)/πθt​(v∣x,y<i)\rho_{i}(v)=\pi_{\theta}(v\mid x,y_{<i})/\pi_{\theta_{t}}(v\mid x,y_{<i}). The per-candidate loss is the PPO-style clipped objective with asymmetric clipping range (1−0.2, 1+0.28)(1-0.2,\,1+0.28) and dual clipping at 33 for negative advantages (Schulman et al., 2017):

ℓi​(v)=max⁡(−Ai​(v)​ρi​(v),−Ai​(v)​clip​(ρi​(v),0.8,1.28)),ℓi​(v)←min⁡(ℓi​(v),−3​Ai​(v))​if ​Ai​(v)<0.\ell_{i}(v)=\max\!\big(-A_{i}(v)\rho_{i}(v),\,-A_{i}(v)\,\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i}(v),0.8,1.28)\big),\quad\ell_{i}(v)\leftarrow\min\!\big(\ell_{i}(v),\,-3A_{i}(v)\big)\ \text{if }A_{i}(v)<0. (10)

Candidate losses are summed over v∈𝒱iv\in\mathcal{V}_{i} to a per-token loss, and per-token losses are averaged over all unmasked response tokens of the mini-batch (“token-mean”). Because the mini-batch equals the rollout batch and a single PPO epoch is used, each rollout batch yields exactly one optimizer step, θ=θt\theta=\theta_{t} when the gradient is formed, ρi​(v)=1\rho_{i}(v)=1 up to floating-point recomputation noise, and the clipping is inactive in effect; the gradient of the surrogate then equals the gradient of Equation 3.

Masking.

Responses whose generation ended by hitting the length cap are flagged at rollout time and excluded from the loss mask entirely (all of their tokens), before token-mean aggregation. Prompts are never trained on.

Per-domain decomposition.

For analysis, the learner performs the backward pass domain by domain: the token-mean loss is restricted to the tokens of domain dd and multiplied by that domain’s share of unmasked tokens, so that the per-domain gradients sum exactly to the batch gradient GtG_{t}. After each domain’s backward pass the per-domain coefficient gradients ⟨Gm(d),τk,m⟩\langle G^{(d)}_{m},\tau_{k,m}\rangle are recorded, without clearing the accumulating weight gradient, and the total coefficient gradient used in Equation 6 is their sum. This decomposition changes neither the weight nor the coefficient update; it only exposes the domain-wise terms discussed in Section 3.2.

Appendix B Update Rule: Implementation Details and Equivalence Conditions

What is stored.

The trainable state consists of the full-precision (FP32) master copy of the student weights (W,ϕ)(W,\phi), sharded across data-parallel workers, the AdamW moments for all of them, the free coefficient table α~\tilde{\alpha} and its Adam moments. BB is never stored. The task vectors are not stored on the accelerator; the base and expert checkpoints are memory-mapped and each τk,m\tau_{k,m} is formed one module at a time when needed.

Order of operations within a step.

(1) Rollout at θt\theta_{t} and teacher scoring. (2) Learner forward/backward producing (G,Gϕ)(G,G_{\phi}), with the per-domain decomposition above. (3) Coefficient gradients ⟨Gm,τk,m⟩\langle G_{m},\tau_{k,m}\rangle are computed from the unclipped sharded gradients, each shard contributing its partial inner product and the partial sums reduced across shards; tied coefficients sum their modules’ values. (4) The full gradient (G,Gϕ)(G,G_{\phi}) is clipped to global norm cWc_{W} and AdamW (decay 00) is stepped on (W,ϕ)(W,\phi). (5) The coefficient gradient is clipped to norm cαc_{\alpha} and Adam (decay 00) is stepped on α~\tilde{\alpha}. (6) The increment ∑kΔ​αk,m​τk,m\sum_{k}\Delta\alpha_{k,m}\tau_{k,m} is added to each FP32 module shard. (7) Both learning-rate schedulers advance. (8) The weights are synchronized to the rollout engine. If the clipped weight-gradient norm or the coefficient-gradient norm is non-finite, steps (4) to (6) are skipped for that batch and no state changes.

Equivalence to optimizing BB.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote Adam with decay zero and a given learning-rate schedule. Its state after tt steps is a function of the gradient sequence G0,…,Gt−1G_{0},\dots,G_{t-1} only. Since ∂ℒt/∂B=∂ℒt/∂W=Gt\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}/\partial B=\partial\mathcal{L}_{t}/\partial W=G_{t}, running 𝒜\mathcal{A} on BB and running it on WW produce the same increments Δt𝒜\Delta^{\mathcal{A}}_{t}, and Wt+1=Wt+Δt𝒜+D​Δ​αtW_{t+1}=W_{t}+\Delta^{\mathcal{A}}_{t}+D\Delta\alpha_{t} is exactly Bt+1+D​αt+1B_{t+1}+D\alpha_{t+1} when Wt=Bt+D​αtW_{t}=B_{t}+D\alpha_{t}. With nonzero decay the AdamW step contains −η​λwd​Wt-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}W_{t} versus −η​λwd​Bt-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}B_{t}, which differ by −η​λwd​D​αt-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}D\alpha_{t}; the equivalence then fails, and the materialized-WW form would shrink the task-vector component. All reported runs use decay 00.

Checkpoints.

Every 25 steps the FP32 weights, optimizer states and the coefficient table are written; the exported model is a standard checkpoint of (W,ϕ)(W,\phi) with no coefficient metadata required for inference. The coefficient trajectory αt\alpha_{t} is stored separately for analysis.

Measured cost.

Table 7 reports the wall-clock and the per-step time for every coefficient granularity. The additional time is in the actor update, which streams the task vectors; rollout generation is the same for all variants. Coarser tying does not reduce this cost, since every granularity reads all task vectors once per step, and the measured differences between granularities reflect how the streaming overlaps with the rest of the step.

Appendix C Experimental Details

Teachers.

At 4B we use the four released IM-MOPD domain teachers. IM-MOPD does not release its 1.7B domain teachers, so we train all four from the same 1.7B reference model following its teacher training procedure: the medical and law teachers by SFT on filtered responses of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and the finance and instruction-following teachers by GRPO for 200 steps. On its own benchmark, each teacher is within one point of the score reported by IM-MOPD (MedQA 58.9958.99 versus 58.558.5, CaseHOLD 70.5270.52 versus 69.669.6, FinQA 62.6662.66 versus 62.462.4, IFBench 46.4446.44 versus 46.446.4). Qwen3-4B has 36 decoder layers and Qwen3-1.7B has 28; with seven projections per layer, module granularity has |ℳ|=252|\mathcal{M}|=252 and 196196 modules and K​|ℳ|=1,008K|\mathcal{M}|=1{,}008 and 784784 coefficients (layer granularity: 144 and 112; model granularity: 4).

Data.

Training prompts come from per-domain pools prepared with the IM-MOPD data pipeline: 13,761 (medical), 31,396 (law), 8,446 (finance) and 11,472 (IF) prompts, 65,075 in total. Batches are drawn with a domain-balanced sampler (32 prompts per domain); apart from the budget balancing of Open-MOPD, no other balancing or reweighting is applied. Evaluation uses the official test splits (1,273, 5,314, 1,147 and 300 items for MedQA, CaseHOLD, FinQA and IFBench). A held-out validation pool is used only by IM-MOPD, for its merge decisions; none of our methods uses it for model selection.

Baselines.

MOPD (SFT warm-up) starts from 62 SFT steps on teacher samples filtered and mixed with the official IM-MOPD pipeline. MOPD (TA init) differs from P2-MOPD only in freezing the mixing coefficients α\alpha; the coefficients-only variant additionally freezes (W,ϕ)(W,\phi).

Training details.

Each step uses one sampled response per prompt (temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 1.01.0), prompts up to 15,872 and responses up to 16,384 tokens; truncated responses are masked from the loss. Each training step is one rollout batch and one optimizer step, after which the weights are synchronized to the rollout engine. The full list of hyperparameters is in Table 10.

Seeds.

The evaluation sampling seeds (42, 43, 44) are the same for every checkpoint. The four checkpoints of one run are not independent repeats and are never pooled as such.

Task-vector projection.

For Figure 4 the displacement of every module from the TA start is projected onto the span of its four task vectors by least squares (Gram pseudo-inverse), so the projection coefficients are in the units of α\alpha; on frozen-weight runs they match α−0.25\alpha-0.25 to within 0.010.01 in module mean. The energy share is the squared norm of the projection divided by the squared norm of the displacement, summed over modules. The per-domain coefficient gradients are the inner products ⟨∇Wℒd,τk,m⟩\langle\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}_{d},\tau_{k,m}\rangle recorded at every step (Appendix A).

Controlled interventions.

Each run in Table 3 differs from the corresponding run of P2-MOPD or MOPD (TA init) in a single setting. The random-direction run replaces each τk,m\tau_{k,m} by an independent Gaussian random tensor rescaled to the same Frobenius norm; it starts from the same TA merge and is supervised by the same teachers, so only the directions spanned by the mixing coefficients change. A further run starts MOPD from the final coefficients of P2-MOPD composed onto the base without its weight updates (medical KL 0.0310.031). It keeps MedQA high (recovery 85.185.1) but leaves FinQA near the TA start (recovery 32%32\%) and ends at 69.869.8 average recovery; the learned-α\alpha point on its own is a poor model (average recovery 28.828.8, below the TA merge). The coefficients therefore have to be learned together with the weights. For the run with αmed\alpha_{\mathrm{med}} frozen, we report the training-side medical KL and the MedQA recovery.

Appendix D Coefficient Learning Rate

Figure 6 and Table 8 sweep ηα\eta_{\alpha} at 1.7B with everything else fixed. A three times smaller value (3×10−33\times 10^{-3}) already gives three quarters of the gain of the main setting over MOPD (TA init) (+10.4+10.4 versus +13.8+13.8 at the end of training) and leads MOPD (TA init) at every checkpoint, so the gain is not a narrow tuning peak. 10−210^{-2} is best; a three times larger value (3×10−23\times 10^{-2}) falls below MOPD (TA init) from step 50 on, because FinQA stays at the level of the TA start.

Start from the base model.

For the base-model start of Section 5 (α0=0\alpha_{0}=0), the average recovery of P2-MOPD with ηα=10−2\eta_{\alpha}=10^{-2} / 3×10−23\times 10^{-2} against MOPD is −7.9-7.9 / 15.615.6 versus −20.0-20.0 at step 25, 41.541.5 / 49.049.0 versus 3.03.0 at step 50, 65.965.9 / 64.964.9 versus 26.626.6 at step 75, and 61.261.2 / 66.266.2 versus −15.7-15.7 at step 100, where the Avg. Score is 51.651.6 / 52.252.2 versus 40.440.4. The final MedQA recovery is 62.862.8 / 98.598.5 versus −261.2-261.2, and the final FinQA recovery is 37.737.7 / 22.922.9 versus 52.452.4.

Appendix E Learned Coefficients

Table 9 lists the coefficients at the end of training. At both scales the medical coefficient grows the most, from 0.250.25 to above 0.60.6, while the other three end between 0.330.33 and 0.460.46.

Appendix F Hyperparameters and Matched Initialization

Matched initialization.

The merged start applies coefficient 0.250.25 for each of the four teachers to every tensor of the model, including embeddings, normalization weights and the output head, using the IM-MOPD merge utility in FP32. P2-MOPD and MOPD (TA init) load this identical checkpoint, and MOPD starts from θ0\theta_{0}. The full list of training hyperparameters is in Table 10.

Appendix G Evaluation Protocol and Endpoints

Harness.

All scores come from the official IM-MOPD evaluation harness (frozen protocol file; same code revision for every method and endpoint). For each item three generations are sampled at temperature 1.01.0 with seeds 42, 43 and 44 and the item score is averaged; the reported score is the mean over items (avg@3). IFBench is scored as prompt-level loose accuracy. Per-domain generation caps are 26,624 tokens (MedQA, CaseHOLD, FinQA) and 32,768 (IFBench); the serving engine limits the context to the model’s configured 32,768 positions, so the effective cap for an item is the minimum of the domain cap and the remaining context.

Recovery and aggregation.

Per-domain recovery is (s−sbase)/span(s-s_{\mathrm{base}})/\text{span}; it can exceed 11 or fall below 00. Average recovery is the unweighted mean over the four domains. Because the spans differ (Table 11), a one-point raw change moves recovery by 9.19.1 points on 4B MedQA but 3.03.0 points on 4B IFBench; raw means are therefore reported next to every average-recovery number.

Seed-paired comparisons.

Pairing P2-MOPD and MOPD (TA init) by seed, the step-25 gap in average recovery is +6.17+6.17 at 4B, with a sd of only 0.070.07 across seeds against a seed sd of ≈0.9\approx 0.9 for either method, and +21.5±2.9+21.5\pm 2.9 at 1.7B. The step-50 checkpoint of P2-MOPD exceeds the final checkpoint of MOPD (TA init) in every seed, by +1.6+1.6, +4.5+4.5 and +21.3+21.3 (4B) and by +10.4+10.4, +11.3+11.3 and +7.1+7.1 (1.7B). At 4B the mean paired gap is +6.2+6.2, +7.8+7.8, +10.0+10.0 and +11.7+11.7 at steps 25, 50, 75 and 100, with a final seed range of +4.1+4.1 to +20.6+20.6; at 1.7B it is largest at step 25 and then stays between +12+12 and +14+14.

IM-MOPD runs.

IM-MOPD is trained with an effective batch of 128 and the same merged start, prompt pools, 100 steps, length caps and evaluation harness as the other methods, and with three training seeds. Its recovery-gated rule is applied at steps 25, 50 and 75 with δ=0.3\delta=0.3 and γ=0.6\gamma=0.6 (4B) or 0.40.4 (1.7B), as in its released configurations; the main results use the pre-merge checkpoint at each step. Table 12 lists, for every seed, the domains merged at each step and the average recovery immediately before and after the merge. A merge changes the average recovery by between −17.2-17.2 and +6.8+6.8 points, and the steps that follow recover most of the larger drops. Its in-training validation (four samples per validation item every 25 steps) is part of its method and is included in its wall-clock. Because a seed also changes which domains pass the validation gate, the IM-MOPD seed variation includes the merge path.
